19       This case comes before the Court on competing motions: Plaintiffs’ motion for 
20  preliminary  injunction,  (ECF  No.  13),  and  Defendants’  (collectively  “Wells  Fargo”) 
21  motion to compel arbitration.  (ECF No. 21.)  These matters are fully briefed and submitted.  
22  For the following reasons, the Court grants Defendants’ motion to compel arbitration, 
23  denies as moot Plaintiffs’  motion for preliminary injunction, and dismisses this case 
24  without prejudice.                                                        
25                                    I.                                      
26                        BACKGROUND AND FACTS                                
27       Plaintiffs Alexandria Mosley, Rejoyce Kemp, Berenice Cisneros, and Bruce Parker 
28  all have, or had at one point, a Wells Fargo checking account (“Account”).  (ECF No. 1, 
1  Compl. ¶¶ 16-19.)  Each Plaintiff was enrolled in an optional overdraft program, Debit 
2  Card Overdraft Service (“DCOS”), offered by Wells Fargo for debit card and ATM 
3  transactions.  (Id. ¶¶ 16-19, 70-73.)  When each Plaintiff became a consumer of Wells 
4  Fargo, they received and agreed to be bound by Wells Fargo’s Deposit Account Agreement 
5  (“Account Agreement”).  (Id. ¶ 1.)1  The Account Agreement governs the relationship 
6  between  Plaintiffs  and  Wells  Fargo,  and  contains  provisions  requiring  arbitration  of 
7  disputes between the parties (“Arbitration Agreement”).  (Def. Mot. at 3 (ECF No. 21-1.)) 
8       In accordance with the Arbitration Agreement, Plaintiffs filed arbitration demands 
9  with AAA.  (ECF No. 13-1 at 3.)  The arbitration demands “seek statutory damages and 
10  return of overdraft fees collected in violation of Regulation E” and “state consumer fraud 
11  laws” that have also been “violated as a result of [Wells Fargo’s] violations of Regulation 
12  E.”    (Declaration  of  Alicia  Baiardo  ISO  Defendant’s  Motion  to  Compel  Arbitration 
13  (“Baiardo Decl.”) ¶ 3, Exs. C-F (ECF No. 22.))  The law firm McCune Law Group, APC 
14  (“MLG”) filed the arbitration demands on behalf of Plaintiffs.  (Pl. Oppo. at 9.)  MLG also 
15  filed nearly identical demands for more than 3,300 additional Wells Fargo consumers.  (Id. 
16  at 10.)  As a result, AAA informed MLG and Wells Fargo that the claims would be subject 
17  to AAA’s Supplementary Rules for Multiple Case Filings (“MCF”).  (Baiardo Decl. ¶ 4, 
18  Ex. G.)  MLG requested that certain demands filed against Wells Fargo “be consolidated 
19  and otherwise subject to AAA’s Supplementary Rules for Multiple Case Filings.”  (Id.)  
20  AAA then informed the parties that AAA’s Consumer Rules (“Consumer Rules”) and 
21  Supplementary Rules would apply to the arbitration demands filed by MLG, and appointed 
22  the Honorable Anita Rae Shapiro as Process Arbitrator (“PA Shapiro”) for the MCF 
23  proceedings.  (Id. ¶ 6, Exs. J and K.)

25

27  the October 15, 2021 Account Agreement, and the Arbitration Agreement for Plaintiff Kemp is contained 
   in the May 9, 2022 Account Agreement.  The parties agree the Arbitration Agreements are identical.  (See 
28

2  behalf of Wells Fargo consumers.  (Def. Mot. at 6 (ECF No. 21-1.))  After reviewing many 
3  of these demands, Wells Fargo felt “MLG was not performing reasonable due diligence to 
4  confirm that claimants were (1) Wells Fargo customers, (2) had enrolled in DCOS (a pre-
5  requisite  to  bringing  their  claims)  or  (3)  had  incurred  any  overdraft  fees  subject  to 
6  Regulation E.”  (Id. at 7.)  As a result, Wells Fargo brought a motion in the arbitration 
7  forum  pursuant  to  Supplementary  Rule  MC-6  (which  provides  the  PA  authority  to 
8  determine filing requirements in MCF proceedings) and asked PA Shapiro to require MLG 
9  “to provide the requisite basic information in the demands it was filing.”  (Id. at 8.)2  On 
10  October 27, 2022, PA Shapiro issued an Order granting in part and denying in part 
11  Defendants’ request (“PA Order”).  (Baiardo Decl. ¶16, Ex. T.)  Specifically, the PA Order 
12  required all demands to “plead, 1) each Claimant’s Wells Fargo account number for the 
13  account at issue, 2) facts to establish each Claimant was enrolled in DCOS during the time 
14  period at issue[,] and 3) facts sufficient to establish that each Claimant incurred overdraft 
15  fees in connection with transactions covered by Regulation E.”  (Id.)     
16       MLG informed AAA and Wells Fargo it objected to the PA Order, planned to 
17  challenge the PA Order in federal court, advised that MLG would continue to file claims 
18  as it had, and requested AAA to stay the proceedings.  (Id. ¶ 17, Ex. V.)  Wells Fargo 
19  argued the PA Order was proper and AAA lacked authority to stay the proceedings.  (Id. ¶ 
20  18, Ex. W.)  AAA declined to withdraw the PA Order and stay proceedings absent 
21  agreement by the parties or an order from the court.  (Id. ¶ 19, Ex. Y.)  
22       Plaintiffs,  who  are  four  of  the  claimants  represented  by  MLG  in  the  MCF 
23  proceedings,  filed  this  lawsuit  on  December  13,  2022.    (See  Compl.  (ECF  No.  1.))  
24  Plaintiffs first cause of action alleges Defendants breached the Account Agreement by

27  identify basic information such as customer account numbers: “i don’t have one”; “Idk”; “xxxxxxxxxx”; 
   “XXX…”; “Not giving my account”; “None”; “999999999”; “N/a”; “[claimant’s last name]”; “Not sure”; 
28                                                                            
1  refusing to pay arbitration fees and prevented Plaintiffs’ arbitration claims from going 
2  forward.  (Id. ¶¶ 83-91.)  Plaintiffs ask the Court to “enter declaratory judgment declaring 
3  that Wells Fargo has breached its arbitration agreement with Plaintiffs, and Plaintiffs are 
4  thus no longer bound by the agreement[,]” (Id. ¶ 90), and to “issue appropriate injunctive 
5  relief staying or terminating the current arbitration proceedings.”  (Id. ¶ 91.)  Plaintiffs’ 
6  second cause of action alleges Defendants violated Regulation E’s “Opt In Rule,” 12 C.F.R. 
7  §§ 1005, et seq., and seeks “declaratory judgment that (1) Wells Fargo violated Regulation 
8  E by failing to obtain Plaintiffs’ lawful consent before enrolling them in DCOS and (2), as 
9  a result, Wells Fargo unlawfully charged Plaintiffs overdraft fees on ATM and one-time 
10  debit card transactions.”  (Id. ¶ 101.)  Plaintiffs third cause of action alleges Defendants 
11  violated California’s Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”) by violating Regulation E.  (Id. ¶¶ 
12  103-11.)  Accordingly, Plaintiffs ask the Court to “award equitable relief . . . in the form 
13  of injunctive relief preventing Wells Fargo from (i) enforcing its arbitration agreement with 
14  Plaintiffs and other current customers unable to obtain arbitration hearings because of 
15  Wells Fargo’s obstruction; (ii) offering the arbitration agreement to those who are not yet 
16  customers,  but  will  open  accounts  in  the  future;  and  (iii)  charging  overdraft  fees  to 
17  Plaintiffs and other customers on Regulation E transactions until Wells Fargo has obtained 
18  affirmative consent through an overdraft disclosure and practices that are consistent with 
19  Regulation E.”  (Id. ¶ 111.)                                              
20                                    II.                                     
21                            LEGAL STANDARD                                  
22       The Federal Arbitration Act (“FAA”), 9 U.S.C. § 1 et seq., governs the enforcement 
23  of arbitration agreements involving interstate commerce.  Am. Express Co. v. Italian Colors 
24  Rest., 570 U.S. 228, 232–33 (2013).  “The overarching purpose of the FAA . . . is to ensure 
25  the enforcement of arbitration agreements according to their terms so as to facilitate 
26  streamlined proceedings.”  AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion, 563 U.S. 333, 344 (2011).  
27  “The FAA ‘leaves no place for the exercise of discretion by the district court, but instead 
28  mandates that district courts shall direct the parties to proceed to arbitration on issues as to 
1  which an arbitration has been signed.’” Kilgore v. KeyBank, Nat. Ass’n., 718 F.3d 1052, 
2  1058 (9th Cir. 2013) (quoting Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc. v. Byrd, 470 U.S. 213, 218 
3  (1985)).  Accordingly, the Court’s role under the FAA is to determine “(1) whether a valid 
4  agreement to arbitrate exists, and if it does, (2) whether the agreement encompasses the 
5  dispute at issue.” Chiron Corp. v. Ortho Diagnostic Sys., Inc., 207 F.3d 1126, 1130 (9th 
6  Cir. 2000).  If both factors are met, the Court must enforce the arbitration agreement 
7  according to its terms.  The burden of proving claims are not suitable for arbitration is on 
8  the party resisting arbitration.  Green Tree Fin. Corp-Ala. v. Randolph, 531 U.S. 79, 91 
9  (2000).  Under the FAA, “any doubts concerning the scope of the arbitrable issues should 
10  be resolved in favor of arbitration.”  Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 
11  460 U.S. 1, 24–25 (1983).                                                 
12                                   III.                                     
13                               DISCUSSION                                   
14       As noted, in deciding whether to compel arbitration, a district court must determine 
15  two gateway issues: “(1) whether there is an agreement to arbitrate between the parties; 
16  and (2) whether the agreement covers the dispute.”  Brennan v. Opus Bank, 796 F.3d 1125, 
17  1130 (9th Cir. 2015) (citing Howsam v. Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc., 537 U.S. 79, 84 
18  (2002)).  “However, these gateway issues can be expressly delegated to the arbitrator where 
19  ‘the parties clearly and unmistakably provide otherwise.’”  Id. (quoting AT & T Techs., Inc. 
20  v. Commc’ns Workers of Am., 475 U.S. 643, 649 (1986)).                    
21  A.   Delegation of Gateway Issues                                         
22       “[L]anguage ‘delegating to the arbitrators the authority to determine the validity or 
23  application of any of the provisions of the arbitration clause [ ] constitutes an agreement to 
24  arbitrate  threshold  issues  concerning  the  arbitration  agreement.’”    Mohamed  v.  Uber 
25  Techs., Inc., 848 F.3d 1201, 1208 (9th Cir. 2016) (quoting Momot v. Mastro, 652 F.3d 982, 
26  988 (9th Cir. 2011)); see also Rent-A-Center, West, Inc. v. Jackson, 561 U.S. 63, 68–69 
27  (2010) (“parties can agree to arbitrate ‘gateway’ questions of ‘arbitrability,’ such as . . . 
28  whether their agreement covers a particular controversy.”).  Where the parties have “clearly 
1  and unmistakably” delegated such gateway issues to the arbitrator, the validity of the 
2  arbitration agreement is a question for the arbitrator to decide, rather than the court.  AT & 
3  T Techs., 475 U.S. at 649.  While “there is a presumption that courts will decide which 
4  issues are arbitrable; the federal policy in favor of arbitration does not extend to deciding 
5  questions of arbitrability.”  Oracle Am., Inc. v. Myriad Grp. A.G., 724 F.3d 1069, 1072 
6  (9th Cir. 2013).                                                          
7       Wells Fargo contends the Arbitration Agreement delegates arbitrability of Plaintiffs’ 
8  claims in the present action to arbitration.  Wells Fargo points out that this Court has 
9  already determined that a nearly identical arbitration provision delegates arbitrability to 
10  arbitration, see Wilson v. Wells Fargo & Co., No. 20-cv-02307, 2022 WL 4125220 (S.D. 
11  Cal.  Sept. 9,  2022),  and that  Plaintiffs affirmatively  acceded  to  AAA’s  authority  by 
12  submitting their demands.  See Nghiem v. NEC Electronic, Inc., 25 F.3d 1437, 1440 (9th 
13  Cir. 1994), cert. denied, 513 U.S. 1044 (1994) (“[o]nce a claimant submits to the authority 
14  of the arbitrator and pursues arbitration, he cannot suddenly change his mind and assert 
15  lack of authority.”)                                                      
16       The Arbitration Agreement states AAA “will hear the dispute between Wells Fargo 
17  and you,” and defines “dispute” as “any unresolved disagreement between Wells Fargo 
18  and you.”  (Arbitration Agreement, ECF No. 22-1 at 35.)  A “dispute” also “include[s] a 
19  disagreement about this Arbitration Agreement’s meaning, application, or enforcement.”  
20  (Id.)  It further states: “If this Arbitration Agreement is in dispute, the arbitrator will decide 
21  whether it is enforceable.”  (Id.)  (Pl. Oppo. at 9 (ECF No. 25.))  These provisions “clearly 
22  and unmistakably” delegate gateway issues of arbitrability to the arbitrator.  
23       Plaintiffs nevertheless argue the relief they seek falls within a carve-out provision of 
24  the Arbitration Agreement, which permits “provisional or ancillary remedies such as 
25  injunctive relief.”  (Id.)  However, such relief is only permitted “on arbitrable claims if 
26  interim  relief  is  necessary  to  preserve  the  status  quo  and  the  meaningfulness  of  the 
27  arbitration process.”  Toyo Tire Holdings of Ams., Inc. v. Cont’l Tire N. Am., Inc., 609 F.3d 
28  975, 981 (9th Cir. 2010).  That is not the case here.                     
1       Plaintiffs seek a “total stay of arbitration proceedings pending a hearing on whether 
2  Defendants  have violated their arbitration agreements with Plaintiffs.”  (Pl. Mot. for 
3  Prelim. Inj. at 1 (ECF No. 13-1.))  This request invites the Court to provide relief sought in 
4  Plaintiffs’ second and third causes of action.  (See Compl. ¶¶ 92-111.)  In their second 
5  cause of action, Plaintiffs ask the Court to issue a declaratory judgment that Wells Fargo 
6  violated Regulation E.  (Id. ¶¶ 92-102.)  This request for relief is neither provisional nor 
7  ancillary; rather, the request goes directly to the merits of a dispute already submitted to 
8  arbitration.  The third cause of action fares no better.  It asks the Court to enjoin Wells 
9  Fargo from enforcing its Arbitration Agreement and charging overdraft fees to Plaintiffs 
10  and other customers.  (Id. ¶¶ 103-111.)  To provide such relief, the Court would have to 
11  determine the merits of the dispute that Plaintiffs have already submitted to arbitration.  
12  Once a party demands arbitration, as here, the party has submitted to the authority of the 
13  arbitral tribunal.  Nghiem, 25 F.3d at 1440.  A party “cannot await the outcome and, after 
14  an unfavorable decision, challenge the authority of the arbitrators” to issue such decisions.  
15  PowerAgent  Inc.  v.  Elec.  Data  Sys.  Corp.,  358  F.3d  1187,  1192  (9th  Cir.  2004).  
16  Accordingly, Plaintiffs cannot now seek to have the entirety of their dispute resolved by 
17  this Court.  These matters have been submitted to arbitration and are properly before that 
18  tribunal.                                                                 
19  B.   The PA Order: Final and Binding, or Procedural and not Reviewable?   
20       An arbitration award is generally subject to judicial review only when it is final and 
21  binding.  Millmen Local 550, United Broth. of Carpenters and Joiners of Am., AFL-CIO v. 
22  Wells Exterior Trim, 828 F. 2d 1373, 1375 (9th Cir. 1987).  The parties dispute whether 
23  the PA Order is “final and binding,” and thus subject to judicial review.  Plaintiffs believe 
24  the PA Order is “final and binding” because the AAA rules state the PA’s decisions “will 
25  be final and binding upon the parties and Merit Arbitrator,” and it “directly impacts 
26  Plaintiffs’ rights to arbitrate their claims.”  (Pl. Oppo at 14 (ECF No. 25.))  In support, 
27  Plaintiffs rely on Southern Seas Navigation Ltd. of Monrovia v. Petroleos Mexicanos of 
28  Mexico City, 606 F.Supp. 692 (S.D.N.Y. 1985).  In Southern Seas, the parties entered 
1  arbitration pursuant to their contract, and submitted among other issues to the arbitrator a 
2  claim for equitable relief removing a Notice of Claim of Lien.  Id. at 693.  The arbitrator 
3  issued an “interim” award, and compared the award to a preliminary injunction, which 
4  reduced the amount of a lien on property before a final determination on the merits.  Id.  
5  The district court reasoned the interim award was “final and binding” and subject to judicial 
6  review because the award required “affirmative action” and would be meaningless if left 
7  unenforced.  Id. at 694.                                                  
8       Unlike in Southern Seas, the PA Order is not an award on the merits but a procedural 
9  order that addresses claim filing requirements in the MCF.  Plaintiffs argue the PA Order 
10  “directly impacts [their] rights to arbitrate” because it “requires information at the pleading 
11  stage that Plaintiffs are unable to obtain.”  (Id. at 15 n.12.)  However, as Wells Fargo notes, 
12  Plaintiffs provided the information required by the PA Order in the subject Complaint, (see 
13  Compl. ¶¶ 16-19), and can do so in the MCF with Plaintiffs’ and other customers’ demands.  
14  As Wells Fargo also notes, when AAA invoiced Wells Fargo for the initial administrative 
15  filing fees associated with the arbitration demands, Wells Fargo paid those invoices on 
16  eight separate occasions for a total amount of $501,075, and will continue to do so with 
17  future AAA invoices.  (Mot. at 7.)                                        
18       Further, it is well-settled that questions of procedure relating to arbitration are not 
19  reviewable by courts.  “In the absence of an express agreement to the contrary, procedural 
20  questions are submitted to the arbitrator, either explicitly or implicitly, along with the 
21  merits of the dispute.”  McKesson Corp. v. Local 150 IBT, 969 F.2d 831, 834 (9th Cir. 
22  1992).    “[P]rocedural  questions which  grow out  of  [a] dispute  and  bear  on  its  final 
23  disposition are presumptively not for the judge, but for an arbitrator, to decide.”  Stolt-
24  Nielsen S.A. v. AnimalFeeds Int’l Corp., 559 U.S. 662, 685 (2010).  Procedural questions 
25  include, for example, “whether grievance procedures or some part of them apply to a 
26  particular dispute, whether such procedures have been followed or excused, or whether the 
27  unexcused failure to follow them avoids the duty to arbitrate.”  John Wiley & Sons, Inc. v. 
28  Livingston, 376 U.S. 543, 558 (1964).  Ultimately, “the basic purpose of arbitration is the 
1   ||speedy  disposition  of  disputes  without  the  expense  and  delay  of  extended  court 
2 || proceedings.”  Jn re Sussex, 781  F.3d  1065,  1072 (9th Cir. 2015) (citation and quotation 
3   |;omitted).   “To  permit  what  is  in  effect  an  appeal  from  an  interlocutory  ruling  of the 
4   ||arbitrator would frustrate this purpose.”  Jd.  Here, the PA Order deals with procedure, 
5   ||namely pleading and filing requirements, to provide an orderly process for the MCF—all 
6   ||based  on  PA  Shapiro’s  interpretation  of the  Supplementary  Rules  to  which the  parties 
7   |;agreed.  As such, the PA Order is not a “final” order under Mil/men Local 550, and is not 
8 || subject to judicial review. 
9   ||C.    Stay or Dismissal of the Subject Case? 
10         Wells Fargo asks the Court to stay this case pending completion of each □□□□□□□□□□□ 
11    arbitration, or in the alternative, dismiss the case without prejudice.  “[A] district court may 
12 || either stay the action or dismiss it outright when .  .  . the court determines that all of the 
13    claims raised in the action are subject to arbitration.”  Johnmohammadi v. Bloomingdale’s, 
14 ||       755 F.3d  1072,  1074 (9th Cir. 2014).  Here, the Court elects to dismiss the subject 
15            without  prejudice  and  allow  the  claims  already  submitted,  and  those  yet  to  be 
16    submitted, in the AAA MCF proceedings to run their course. 
17                                            IV. 
18                              CONCLUSION AND ORDER 
19         For  these  reasons,  Defendant’s  motion  to  compel  arbitration  is  GRANTED, 
20 || Plaintiffs’ motion for preliminary injunction is DENIED as moot, and the case is dismissed 
21 || without prejudice. 
22         IT IS SO ORDERED. 
23 || Dated: May 1, 2023 
24

8  E by failing to obtain Plaintiffs’ lawful consent before enrolling them in DCOS and (2), as 
9  a result, Wells Fargo unlawfully charged Plaintiffs overdraft fees on ATM and one-time 
10  debit card transactions.”  (Id. ¶ 101.)  Plaintiffs third cause of action alleges Defendants 
11  violated California’s Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”) by violating Regulation E.  (Id. ¶¶ 
12  103-11.)  Accordingly, Plaintiffs ask the Court to “award equitable relief . . . in the form 
13  of injunctive relief preventing Wells Fargo from (i) enforcing its arbitration agreement with 
14  Plaintiffs and other current customers unable to obtain arbitration hearings because of 
15  Wells Fargo’s obstruction; (ii) offering the arbitration agreement to those who are not yet 
16  customers,  but  will  open  accounts  in  the  future;  and  (iii)  charging  overdraft  fees  to 
17  Plaintiffs and other customers on Regulation E transactions until Wells Fargo has obtained 
18  affirmative consent through an overdraft disclosure and practices that are consistent with 
19  Regulation E.”  (Id. ¶ 111.)                                              
20                                    II.                                     
21                            LEGAL STANDARD                                  
22       The Federal Arbitration Act (“FAA”),
9 U.S.C. § 1
 et seq., governs the enforcement 
23  of arbitration agreements involving interstate commerce.  Am. Express Co. v. Italian Colors 
24  Rest.,
570 U.S. 228
, 232–33 (2013).  “The overarching purpose of the FAA . . . is to ensure 
25  the enforcement of arbitration agreements according to their terms so as to facilitate 
26  streamlined proceedings.”  AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion,
563 U.S. 333
, 344 (2011).  
27  “The FAA ‘leaves no place for the exercise of discretion by the district court, but instead 
28  mandates that district courts shall direct the parties to proceed to arbitration on issues as to 
1  which an arbitration has been signed.’” Kilgore v. KeyBank, Nat. Ass’n.,
718 F.3d 1052
, 
2  1058 (9th Cir. 2013) (quoting Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc. v. Byrd,
470 U.S. 213
, 218 
3  (1985)).  Accordingly, the Court’s role under the FAA is to determine “(1) whether a valid 
4  agreement to arbitrate exists, and if it does, (2) whether the agreement encompasses the 
5  dispute at issue.” Chiron Corp. v. Ortho Diagnostic Sys., Inc.,
207 F.3d 1126, 1130
 (9th 
6  Cir. 2000).  If both factors are met, the Court must enforce the arbitration agreement 
7  according to its terms.  The burden of proving claims are not suitable for arbitration is on 
8  the party resisting arbitration.  Green Tree Fin. Corp-Ala. v. Randolph,
531 U.S. 79
, 91 
9  (2000).  Under the FAA, “any doubts concerning the scope of the arbitrable issues should 
10  be resolved in favor of arbitration.”  Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 
11
460 U.S. 1
, 24–25 (1983).                                                 
12                                   III.                                     
13                               DISCUSSION                                   
14       As noted, in deciding whether to compel arbitration, a district court must determine 
15  two gateway issues: “(1) whether there is an agreement to arbitrate between the parties; 
16  and (2) whether the agreement covers the dispute.”  Brennan v. Opus Bank,
796 F.3d 1125
, 
17  1130 (9th Cir. 2015) (citing Howsam v. Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc.,
537 U.S. 79
, 84 
18  (2002)).  “However, these gateway issues can be expressly delegated to the arbitrator where 
19  ‘the parties clearly and unmistakably provide otherwise.’”
Id.
 (quoting AT & T Techs., Inc. 
20  v. Commc’ns Workers of Am.,
475 U.S. 643, 649
 (1986)).                    
21  A.   Delegation of Gateway Issues                                         
22       “[L]anguage ‘delegating to the arbitrators the authority to determine the validity or 
23  application of any of the provisions of the arbitration clause [ ] constitutes an agreement to 
24  arbitrate  threshold  issues  concerning  the  arbitration  agreement.’”    Mohamed  v.  Uber 
25  Techs., Inc.,
848 F.3d 1201, 1208
 (9th Cir. 2016) (quoting Momot v. Mastro,
652 F.3d 982
, 
26  988 (9th Cir. 2011)); see also Rent-A-Center, West, Inc. v. Jackson,
561 U.S. 63
, 68–69 
27  (2010) (“parties can agree to arbitrate ‘gateway’ questions of ‘arbitrability,’ such as . . . 
28  whether their agreement covers a particular controversy.”).  Where the parties have “clearly 
1  and unmistakably” delegated such gateway issues to the arbitrator, the validity of the 
2  arbitration agreement is a question for the arbitrator to decide, rather than the court.  AT & 
3  T Techs.,
475 U.S. at 649
.  While “there is a presumption that courts will decide which 
4  issues are arbitrable; the federal policy in favor of arbitration does not extend to deciding 
5  questions of arbitrability.”  Oracle Am., Inc. v. Myriad Grp. A.G.,
724 F.3d 1069
, 1072 
6  (9th Cir. 2013).                                                          
7       Wells Fargo contends the Arbitration Agreement delegates arbitrability of Plaintiffs’ 
8  claims in the present action to arbitration.  Wells Fargo points out that this Court has 
9  already determined that a nearly identical arbitration provision delegates arbitrability to 
10  arbitration, see Wilson v. Wells Fargo & Co., No. 20-cv-02307,
2022 WL 4125220
 (S.D. 
11  Cal.  Sept. 9,  2022),  and that  Plaintiffs affirmatively  acceded  to  AAA’s  authority  by 
12  submitting their demands.  See Nghiem v. NEC Electronic, Inc.,
25 F.3d 1437, 1440
 (9th 
13  Cir. 1994), cert. denied,
513 U.S. 1044
 (1994) (“[o]nce a claimant submits to the authority 
14  of the arbitrator and pursues arbitration, he cannot suddenly change his mind and assert 
15  lack of authority.”)                                                      
16       The Arbitration Agreement states AAA “will hear the dispute between Wells Fargo 
17  and you,” and defines “dispute” as “any unresolved disagreement between Wells Fargo 
18  and you.”  (Arbitration Agreement, ECF No. 22-1 at 35.)  A “dispute” also “include[s] a 
19  disagreement about this Arbitration Agreement’s meaning, application, or enforcement.”  
20  (Id.)  It further states: “If this Arbitration Agreement is in dispute, the arbitrator will decide 
21  whether it is enforceable.”  (Id.)  (Pl. Oppo. at 9 (ECF No. 25.))  These provisions “clearly 
22  and unmistakably” delegate gateway issues of arbitrability to the arbitrator.  
23       Plaintiffs nevertheless argue the relief they seek falls within a carve-out provision of 
24  the Arbitration Agreement, which permits “provisional or ancillary remedies such as 
25  injunctive relief.”  (Id.)  However, such relief is only permitted “on arbitrable claims if 
26  interim  relief  is  necessary  to  preserve  the  status  quo  and  the  meaningfulness  of  the 
27  arbitration process.”  Toyo Tire Holdings of Ams., Inc. v. Cont’l Tire N. Am., Inc.,
609 F.3d 28 975, 981
 (9th Cir. 2010).  That is not the case here.                     
1       Plaintiffs seek a “total stay of arbitration proceedings pending a hearing on whether 
2  Defendants  have violated their arbitration agreements with Plaintiffs.”  (Pl. Mot. for 
3  Prelim. Inj. at 1 (ECF No. 13-1.))  This request invites the Court to provide relief sought in 
4  Plaintiffs’ second and third causes of action.  (See Compl. ¶¶ 92-111.)  In their second 
5  cause of action, Plaintiffs ask the Court to issue a declaratory judgment that Wells Fargo 
6  violated Regulation E.  (Id. ¶¶ 92-102.)  This request for relief is neither provisional nor 
7  ancillary; rather, the request goes directly to the merits of a dispute already submitted to 
8  arbitration.  The third cause of action fares no better.  It asks the Court to enjoin Wells 
9  Fargo from enforcing its Arbitration Agreement and charging overdraft fees to Plaintiffs 
10  and other customers.  (Id. ¶¶ 103-111.)  To provide such relief, the Court would have to 
11  determine the merits of the dispute that Plaintiffs have already submitted to arbitration.  
12  Once a party demands arbitration, as here, the party has submitted to the authority of the 
13  arbitral tribunal.  Nghiem,
25 F.3d at 1440
.  A party “cannot await the outcome and, after 
14  an unfavorable decision, challenge the authority of the arbitrators” to issue such decisions.  
15  PowerAgent  Inc.  v.  Elec.  Data  Sys.  Corp.,
358 F.3d 1187, 1192
  (9th  Cir.  2004).  
16  Accordingly, Plaintiffs cannot now seek to have the entirety of their dispute resolved by 
17  this Court.  These matters have been submitted to arbitration and are properly before that 
18  tribunal.                                                                 
19  B.   The PA Order: Final and Binding, or Procedural and not Reviewable?   
20       An arbitration award is generally subject to judicial review only when it is final and 
21  binding.  Millmen Local 550, United Broth. of Carpenters and Joiners of Am., AFL-CIO v. 
22  Wells Exterior Trim,
828 F. 2d 1373, 1375
 (9th Cir. 1987).  The parties dispute whether 
23  the PA Order is “final and binding,” and thus subject to judicial review.  Plaintiffs believe 
24  the PA Order is “final and binding” because the AAA rules state the PA’s decisions “will 
25  be final and binding upon the parties and Merit Arbitrator,” and it “directly impacts 
26  Plaintiffs’ rights to arbitrate their claims.”  (Pl. Oppo at 14 (ECF No. 25.))  In support, 
27  Plaintiffs rely on Southern Seas Navigation Ltd. of Monrovia v. Petroleos Mexicanos of 
28  Mexico City,
606 F.Supp. 692
 (S.D.N.Y. 1985).  In Southern Seas, the parties entered 
1  arbitration pursuant to their contract, and submitted among other issues to the arbitrator a 
2  claim for equitable relief removing a Notice of Claim of Lien.
Id. at 693
.  The arbitrator 
3  issued an “interim” award, and compared the award to a preliminary injunction, which 
4  reduced the amount of a lien on property before a final determination on the merits.
Id.
  
5  The district court reasoned the interim award was “final and binding” and subject to judicial 
6  review because the award required “affirmative action” and would be meaningless if left 
7  unenforced.
Id. at 694
.                                                  
8       Unlike in Southern Seas, the PA Order is not an award on the merits but a procedural 
9  order that addresses claim filing requirements in the MCF.  Plaintiffs argue the PA Order 
10  “directly impacts [their] rights to arbitrate” because it “requires information at the pleading 
11  stage that Plaintiffs are unable to obtain.”  (Id. at 15 n.12.)  However, as Wells Fargo notes, 
12  Plaintiffs provided the information required by the PA Order in the subject Complaint, (see 
13  Compl. ¶¶ 16-19), and can do so in the MCF with Plaintiffs’ and other customers’ demands.  
14  As Wells Fargo also notes, when AAA invoiced Wells Fargo for the initial administrative 
15  filing fees associated with the arbitration demands, Wells Fargo paid those invoices on 
16  eight separate occasions for a total amount of $501,075, and will continue to do so with 
17  future AAA invoices.  (Mot. at 7.)                                        
18       Further, it is well-settled that questions of procedure relating to arbitration are not 
19  reviewable by courts.  “In the absence of an express agreement to the contrary, procedural 
20  questions are submitted to the arbitrator, either explicitly or implicitly, along with the 
21  merits of the dispute.”  McKesson Corp. v. Local 150 IBT,
969 F.2d 831, 834
 (9th Cir. 
22  1992).    “[P]rocedural  questions which  grow out  of  [a] dispute  and  bear  on  its  final 
23  disposition are presumptively not for the judge, but for an arbitrator, to decide.”  Stolt-
24  Nielsen S.A. v. AnimalFeeds Int’l Corp.,
559 U.S. 662, 685
 (2010).  Procedural questions 
25  include, for example, “whether grievance procedures or some part of them apply to a 
26  particular dispute, whether such procedures have been followed or excused, or whether the 
27  unexcused failure to follow them avoids the duty to arbitrate.”  John Wiley & Sons, Inc. v. 
28  Livingston,
376 U.S. 543, 558
 (1964).  Ultimately, “the basic purpose of arbitration is the 
1   ||speedy  disposition  of  disputes  without  the  expense  and  delay  of  extended  court 
2 || proceedings.”  Jn re Sussex,
781 F.3d 1065, 1072
 (9th Cir. 2015) (citation and quotation 
3   |;omitted).   “To  permit  what  is  in  effect  an  appeal  from  an  interlocutory  ruling  of the 
4   ||arbitrator would frustrate this purpose.”  Jd.  Here, the PA Order deals with procedure, 
5   ||namely pleading and filing requirements, to provide an orderly process for the MCF—all 
6   ||based  on  PA  Shapiro’s  interpretation  of the  Supplementary  Rules  to  which the  parties 
7   |;agreed.  As such, the PA Order is not a “final” order under Mil/men Local 550, and is not 
8 || subject to judicial review. 
9   ||C.    Stay or Dismissal of the Subject Case? 
10         Wells Fargo asks the Court to stay this case pending completion of each □□□□□□□□□□□ 
11    arbitration, or in the alternative, dismiss the case without prejudice.  “[A] district court may 
12 || either stay the action or dismiss it outright when .  .  . the court determines that all of the 
13    claims raised in the action are subject to arbitration.”  Johnmohammadi v. Bloomingdale’s, 
14 ||
755 F.3d 1072, 1074
 (9th Cir. 2014).  Here, the Court elects to dismiss the subject 
15            without  prejudice  and  allow  the  claims  already  submitted,  and  those  yet  to  be 
16    submitted, in the AAA MCF proceedings to run their course.
